  **Drawn** is built and tested: a polygon or rectangle drawn on the map is written into the saved

  untouched filters intact, and a refused edit leaving the file byte for byte as it was. **Excluded**

  **Named** is not. A drawn shape is saved as `{type: polygon, geometry: ...}` with no name, so a
  file with three drawn areas reads as three drawn areas rather than as "east side", "the flats" and
  "near the school". The saved-search format supports a `name` on an area and this does not set one.

  **Edited** is partly not. Leaflet.draw's edit control is enabled, so a shape can be reshaped and
  saved again, but there is no way to change one shape's name or its included-or-excluded sense
  without deleting it and drawing it again.

  Why it stopped here: both missing halves are the same small piece of interface, a per-shape panel
  with a name field and an in-or-out control, and neither changes what the tool can express. The
  geometry, which is the part a terminal cannot produce and the reason this surface exists at all,
  round-trips.

  Routed: remediation, and it is one task rather than a design question. Recorded rather than
  quietly counted as done, because AC-2 says three verbs and this delivers one and a half.

- opened gap-003 [unrequested] code:"the guard against the browser, and four things that came with

  Four things the spec never asks for, each of which the pre-build check or the build itself made
  necessary:

  **The guard** (`Host`, `Origin`, and a header on anything that changes something). The spec asks
  for the bind address and nothing else, and the bind address settles which machines can reach this
  and nothing about which pages can. Every page the person has open can send a request to a loopback
  port. Raised at the pre-build check as B-1 and built there rather than discovered later.

  **The tile setting**, off by default. Raised at the same gate as B-2: a slippy map has a tile
  server, `product-global.md` lists four kinds of outbound traffic and a tile server is a fifth. The
  map draws without a background and one line says what turning one on costs.

  **`homescout show` and `homescout areas`.** This feature introduced five capabilities the core did
  not have, and product invariant 5 says every capability is reachable from both surfaces. Without
  these two, the browser would have become the only way to see a property in full or to write a note
  about a town.

  **`Store.open(shared=True)` and a lock.** SQLite refuses a connection used from a thread other
  than the one that opened it, and a web server hands requests to worker threads. The interface is
  the one caller that passes the flag and the one that serializes access, which is what makes it
  safe. Found by running the real server rather than by reading, because the tests had been reaching
  for a shared store explicitly.

  Routed: a human decision on all four. The recommendation is to legitimize the first two as
  additions to AC-15, and to record the last two as what they are, which is the cost of the feature
  rather than the feature. Recorded, not self-applied.

## What was checked and found clean

- **The table's shape was decided by measurement rather than by taste, and then measured again.**
  Before anything was designed: 5,000 rows of 32 columns in Chrome, a full-DOM table taking 3,766ms
  to redraw after a sort against a 200ms budget, and a windowed one taking 25ms. After it was built:
  the same 5,000 rows, served by a real server over loopback to a real browser, interactive in well
  under three seconds, sorting and filtering inside the budget, with fewer than five thousand
  elements in the page instead of a hundred and sixty-five thousand.
- **Non-negotiable 8 is enforced twice.** A source scan asserts nothing in `web` imports the store,
  the runner, the rule engine, the export, the sources, the merge, the extraction or the enrichment;
  and every action is performed through HTTP and again through `api`, with the whole database
  compared. A capability missing from `api` is a capability this interface cannot have, which is
  what makes the command line get it too.
- **The security requirement about listing text is structural.** There is one way to build an
  element and it uses `textContent`; no `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`,
  `document.write` or `eval` anywhere; no template literal that produces markup; and every anchor
  goes through the one helper that checks its target for `http` or `https`. A description containing
  a script tag is a description containing the characters of one, checked in a real browser.
- **AC-6's failure mode is proved, not described.** A save is forced to fail in a real browser and
  the row is checked for keeping the typed value, saying "not saved" in words as well as colour, and
  not claiming to have saved.
- **AC-3's round trip is delegated rather than reimplemented.** The interface never writes YAML. A
  drawn shape is saved by handing the core the whole areas list, and a test asserts that a comment
  and an untouched filter both survive, and that a refused edit leaves the file byte for byte.
- **AC-15 is tested against a routable address rather than read out of a constant**, and the command
  line has no option that could move it, which is the stronger half.
- **AC-16 is bytes.** Each served asset is compared to the file in the repository, and the vendored
  map library is verified against a manifest recording every file's version, source and SHA-256,
  which is the provenance a lock file gives and hand-vendored JavaScript usually has none of.
- **Keyboard operation is designed and then driven.** The table is a grid with roving focus and the
  windowed rendering keeps the focused cell in the page; an inline edit is made in a real browser
  with keys alone and read back out of the store afterwards.
- **Two defects were found by looking at the real thing.** A property's provenance listed the same
  source row once per run it had been seen in, which is exactly what a bad merge looks like on the
  one panel that exists to tell a real record from a bad merge; and an enriched boolean printed as
  `False` in the terminal instead of `no`. Neither was caught by any test, and both were obvious in
  one reading.

- opened gap-005 [unrequested] code:"three changes to how a saved search file is written"

  Evidence: `search/document.py` `remove`, `_same`, and `Document.newline`;
  `search/definition.py` `DEFAULTS_OUT`; `tests/test_searches_document.py`
  `test_a_file_written_on_windows_keeps_its_line_endings` and
  `test_an_edit_that_changes_nothing_writes_nothing`.

  Three behaviours the saved-search feature's spec does not state, all forced by this surface and
  all changes to a file format another feature owns:

  **A key set back to its default is removed rather than written.** Pausing and resuming a search
  otherwise leaves `paused: false` in the file forever, and archiving and bringing it back leaves
  two such lines. Absent and default are the same state for `paused`, `archived` and
  `exclude_areas`, and only for those: a filter at its widest value is not the same as no filter,
  and is deliberately not on that list.

  **An assignment that changes nothing changes nothing.** The map hands the core the whole areas
  list on every save, so without this, opening a search and pressing save rewrote a flow map written
  on one line into a block map written on three. Nobody edited it; it just passed through.

  **Line endings survive.** A file written on Windows ends its lines with a carriage return, and
  every save was normalizing the whole file to the other convention, which turns a one-line change
  into a diff touching every line.

  Routed: a human decision, and the recommendation is to legitimize all three as additions to the
  saved-search feature's round-trip criterion rather than to leave them recorded only here. They are
  the same promise that feature already makes, applied to three cases nobody had hit yet. Recorded,
  not self-applied.

## What was checked and found clean, run 3

- **Parity is a test rather than a claim.** The command line's own parser is walked, every command
  it exposes is looked up in a table naming the route that reaches the same core operation, and the
  test fails both ways: a command with no entry, and an entry for a command that no longer exists.
  Sixteen commands, sixteen entries, plus the four capabilities the terminal carries as a flag.
- **Nothing new was added to the browser that the core did not gain first.** The import scan that
  enforces non-negotiable 8 still passes with the seventh surface in place, which means pause,
  archive, duplicate, run-everything, the settings write and the export form are all operations on
  `api` and the command line reaches every one of them.
- **The settings surface cannot write a credential and does not display one.** The refusal is on
  any name containing KEY, TOKEN, PASSWORD or SECRET, tested from inside and over HTTP, and the
  report says whether a credential is present without ever carrying its value. The writable set is
  a fixed list of six names.
- **Three defects were found by using the thing rather than by testing it.** The settings write
  went to a staging file that was never renamed, so every save from the interface was lost in
  silence while the page said "Saved"; the same write only reached the file, so a setting would not
  have taken effect until somebody restarted the server; and the saved-search list never reported
  `paused` or `archived`, so pausing a search from the list correctly stopped it running and
  visibly did nothing at all. The first two are why `test_a_setting_written_here_lands_in_the_file_and_takes_effect`
  asserts both halves; the third is why the list's payload is now asserted.
- **The map's default was wrong and the owner said so.** It drew no background by default, for a
  privacy reason that is real and is still stated, and the result was a blank grey box. The default
  is unchanged; what changed is that the box now says what is missing, draws a labelled coordinate
  grid to work over, and offers the one click that fixes it with the cost stated beside the offer.
  The trade is the same trade; the person making it can now see it.

implemented: AC-1 through AC-27

- opened gap-006 [unrequested] code:"deletion, and the two things it refuses to delete"

  Evidence: `search/definition.py` `delete`, `restore`, `deleted`, `DELETED`; `api.delete_search`;
  `web/app.py` `DELETE /api/searches/{name}`; `tests/test_web_parity.py`
  `test_deleting_a_search_removes_nothing_a_run_recorded`.

  Recorded here rather than counted as ordinary work because deletion is the one operation whose
  obvious reading collides with a non-negotiable, and the collision is settled in code rather than
  in a person remembering.

  **What it deletes**: the definition's place in the catalogue. Out of the list, skipped by a run
  of everything, not found by name. That is the whole of what was asked for.

  **What it will not delete, first**: the definition itself. The file moves to `searches/deleted/`
  and both surfaces offer it back. A definition is something somebody wrote, the areas are usually
  the part that took longest, and nothing is gained by making this final.

  **What it cannot delete, second**: anything a run recorded. Non-negotiable 2 and product
  invariant 1 make snapshot history append-only, so the properties, their price history and any
  judgment written on them survive, and the answer reports the number of runs kept so nobody
  believes otherwise. The test asserts the whole database is unchanged, byte for byte, which is the
  form that cannot rot: a future edit that started deleting rows would fail it.

  Routed: covered by AC-27 as of this run, so this is a note about where a rule was enforced rather
  than an open question.

## What was checked and found clean, run 4

- **The refusal to overwrite on restore.** Deleting `portales`, making a new `portales`, then
  restoring is the sequence that silently destroys work, and it is refused rather than resolved.
- **Deletion is a capability, so both surfaces have it.** `homescout searches delete` and
  `searches restore` exist alongside the routes, and the parity test that walks the terminal's own
  parser covers them the same way it covers everything else.
- **The confirmation is not a browser dialog.** A modal is dismissed by reflex; the button becomes
  "Yes, delete <name>" beside a Cancel, with the two limits stated in the panel that appears with
  it, so the consequence is read at the moment of the decision rather than in this file.
- **A read never writes.** Prompted by finding `archived: true` in the owner's own definition after
  a session of clicking: every read operation a page load performs was run against a scratch
  definition and the file was compared byte for byte afterwards. Unchanged. The stray key was
  residue from that clicking, not from the tool.
